name: Nnam
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Crabb, David W. 1965. Ekoid Bantu Languages of Ogoja, Eastern Nigeria. Part I: Introduction, Phonology and Comparative Vocabulary. (West African Language Monographs 4.) Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. xii+108 pp.
catalog_locator: p. 6 (Minor Sub-group T-U: language T = Nnam, language U = Ekajuk); p. 8 ('The Nnam language'); p. 23 (Tone: definition, four contrastive tones + fifth Mid 'especially in languages N, O, P, T, and U'); p. 25 (coordinate nuclei, 'greater prominence', sub-group t-u).
catalog_quote: MINOR SUB-GROUP T-U consisting of language T: Nnam and language U: Ekajuk. ... TONE is here defined as the distribution of vocal tension over the syllable. ... tone also has a LOCUS within the syllable determined on contrastive grounds. When two utterances such as fèb and fêb ('fan it' and 'jump') are contrasted, it is precisely the syllabic centre, the most prominent part of the syllable which alone is capable of bearing the contrast. Therefore, this part of the syllable, which is the syllable peak in Hockett's terms, is regarded as the TONE-BEARING segment. Every nucleus must bear a tone, of which there are four contrastive possibilities in the Ekoid Bantu Languages. These possibilities ... 1. HIGH: a level of relatively greatest vocal tension; 2. Low: a level (or a rapidly fading level, if final) of relatively lessened vocal tension; 3. FALLING: a rapid lessening of vocal tension from an initial level of some high intensity; and 4. RISING: a rapid increase of vocal tension, or a maintaining the original level if final. To these four possibilities a fifth has been added, especially in languages N, O, P, T, and U on grounds of dia-phonemic contrast: 5. MID: a level of relatively greater vocal tension.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nnam (Crabb's language T) is analysed, like all Ekoid Bantu languages, as a syllable-tone language: every syllable nucleus carries one of High, Low, Falling, Rising, and (notably in Nde, Nselle, Nta, Nnam, Ekajuk) Mid. No statement about word stress or accent placement is made anywhere in the indexed text ('stress' = 0 hits); Blench's Ekoid ms likewise gives only 'High, Low, Rising, Falling and Downstep tones'.
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; Crabb notes coordinate complex syllable peaks characteristic of sub-group t-u (Nnam, Ekajuk) in which 'neither one of them possesses greater prominence than does the other' (p.25), a remark about vowel sequences, not word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone domain = the syllable (Crabb p.23: 'its domain is fixed, i.e. the syllable'); statement is pan-Ekoid with Nnam explicitly among the mid-tone languages; evidence is snippet-level (archive.org FTS + Google Books search-within), the monograph itself was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Crabb 1965 treats Nnam as his 'language T' (Minor Sub-group T-U = Nnam + Ekajuk; forms from the Nnam Clan, Ikom Division, pop. 5,690 in 1953). Yoder et al. 2008 group Ekajuk/Nnam as one cluster; the only dedicated phonology in the cluster is for the sister language Ekajuk (ekaj1238: Kleiner & Kleiner 1976), not Nnam. Blench's ms statement is for Ekoid (and Mbe) as a whole, not Nnam specifically.
